clinicalPearls: Refers to intraocular haemorrhage, most often vitreous or pre-retinal, occurring in association with subarachnoid or other intracranial haemorrhage or an acute rise in intracranial pressure
The haemorrhage may be unilateral or bilateral and can involve the vitreous, the sub-hyaloid or sub-internal limiting membrane space, or the retina itself
It is frequently discovered when a neurologically recovering patient reports blurred vision or floaters
Its presence is a marker of the severity of the intracranial event and is associated with higher mortality
Fundus examination and, when the media are opaque, B-scan ultrasound establish the diagnosis
Management is observation for spontaneous clearance, with vitrectomy considered for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage
In young children, early vitrectomy is important to prevent deprivation amblyopia
reference.pathophysiology: An abrupt rise in intracranial pressure, typically from subarachnoid haemorrhage, is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath to compress the central retinal vein and the retinochoroidal venous anastomoses. The resulting acute venous congestion and stasis rupture peripapillary and retinal capillaries, releasing blood into the retina, the pre-retinal spaces and the vitreous. The intraocular blood therefore arises locally rather than tracking directly from the cranial cavity.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to characterise the intraocular haemorrhage
Neuroimaging with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging for the intracranial haemorrhage
Optical coherence tomography to localise pre-retinal or sub-internal limiting membrane blood
B-scan ultrasound when the media are too opaque for a fundus view
Coordination with neurosurgery and neurology for the underlying condition
redFlags: Reduced consciousness or neurological deterioration from the underlying intracranial haemorrhage
Suspected non-accidental injury in an infant
Signs of persistently raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: The visual prognosis is often good once the haemorrhage clears spontaneously or after vitrectomy, but the overall outcome is dominated by the severity of the underlying neurological injury.
pitfalls: Overlooking the ocular findings in an unconscious or sedated patient
Failing to recognise an underlying intracranial haemorrhage when the eye signs present first
Delaying vitrectomy in a young child at risk of amblyopia
Assuming the haemorrhage is due to a simple Valsalva effort
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
management: Prioritise treatment of the underlying subarachnoid or intracranial haemorrhage and raised intracranial pressure with neurosurgery and neurology
Observe most intraocular haemorrhage for spontaneous clearance, which commonly occurs over weeks to months
Perform pars plana vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage, dense bilateral involvement, or where earlier visual rehabilitation is needed
Consider earlier vitrectomy in affected children to prevent deprivation amblyopia
Monitor for the complications of retinal detachment, epiretinal membrane and raised intraocular pressure during follow-up
Coordinate ophthalmology follow-up with the neurosurgical and neurological team managing the primary injury
